content: Cysticercosis, in its larval (metacestode) form, can infect human and pig tissues. This parasitic disease is predominantly found in resource-limited regions of Latin America, sub-Saharan Africa, and parts of East, South, and Southeast Asia. These areas often have free-roaming pigs, open defecation practices, poor sanitation, and limited health education. When the central nervous system is affected, the condition is referred to as neurocysticercosis, which is the most significant human disease caused by Taenia solium. Neurocysticercosis is a leading cause of acquired epilepsy in low-income countries, where epilepsy affects approximately 50 million people globally. A 2010 meta-analysis revealed that neurocysticercosis lesions were detected in imaging studies in about 30% of epilepsy patients in T. solium-endemic areas. In rare cases, the proportion of epilepsy patients with neurocysticercosis has been reported to be as high as 57% to 70%. Beyond seizures, neurocysticercosis can lead to hydrocephalus, a potentially fatal condition if untreated. The disease is estimated to account for 8 million disability-adjusted life years (DALYs), though this may be an underestimate due to limited neuroimaging data for accurate diagnosis. The economic and social costs of T. solium infections are significant, as infected pigs and humans face financial losses, stigma, and discrimination. The life cycle of T. solium involves pigs as intermediate hosts. Humans acquire the adult tapeworm (taeniasis) by consuming raw or undercooked pork containing viable cysticerci (larval forms). These cysticerci develop into adult tapeworms in the human intestine. Taeniasis is often asymptomatic or associated with mild gastrointestinal symptoms such as abdominal pain, nausea, diarrhea, or constipation. Pigs become infected by ingesting T. solium eggs or proglottids shed in the feces of infected humans. Humans can also develop cysticercosis by ingesting T. solium eggs through fecal-oral contamination or consuming food or water contaminated with infected human feces. The ingested eggs develop into larvae, which can encyst in muscles, skin, eyes, and the central nervous system. In some cases, individuals may simultaneously have both taeniasis and cysticercosis. Porcine cysticercosis, while often asymptomatic in pigs, can reduce the value of pigs and pork products, leading to carcass condemnation during meat inspection. Heavily infected pigs may experience seizures, as suggested by recent research. The World Health Organization (WHO) classifies T. solium-related taeniasis and cysticercosis as neglected tropical diseases. Endemic areas are defined by the presence or likelihood of the full T. solium life cycle. Control strategies include treating human taeniasis, mass treatment and vaccination of pigs, community health education, improved sanitation (eliminating open defecation), better pig husbandry (preventing free-roaming pigs), and enhanced meat inspection and handling practices. Treating human taeniasis is a core intervention to reduce the risk of neurocysticercosis transmission. However, comprehensive control programs require a One Health approach, integrating human, animal, and environmental health sectors. Preventive chemotherapy (PC) programs can be implemented as public health interventions, using drugs like niclosamide, praziquantel, or albendazole. These drugs are listed in the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines and are effective against taeniasis. However, the optimal drug and dosage for PC in T. solium control remain uncertain. The WHO has developed guidelines for PC to control T. solium taeniasis, providing evidence-based recommendations on drug choice, dosage, and implementation strategies. These guidelines aim to support national programs in endemic areas and inform research priorities to strengthen future recommendations. The treatment of neurocysticercosis, however, is a separate and complex subject addressed in a different WHO guideline. The guideline development process followed WHO's standard methods, ensuring transparency and evidence-based recommendations. It involved systematic reviews, expert consultations, and the participation of stakeholders from endemic regions. The recommendations were formulated considering the balance of benefits and harms, evidence certainty, resource implications, feasibility, equity, and stakeholder acceptability. The process aimed for consensus among guideline development group members, with full agreement achieved on the final recommendations.
